title: Comforted to comfort (2 Corinthians 1:3–4)
hook: the God of all comfort comforts us so we can comfort others

segments.voice: Yesterday, light affliction: the outward self wearing out, the inward one made new. Your line was renewed day by day. Did you do your one small renewing thing? Day one thousand four hundred seventeen.

Two women at a kitchen table. One lost her husband last month, and the house is full of flowers she doesn't know what to do with. The other lost hers years ago. She doesn't make a speech. She knows which casseroles freeze well. She knows that the second month can be harder than the first, when the cards stop coming. She knows not to say he's in a better place unless she's asked. Nobody taught her that in a class. She learned it at her own kitchen table, from someone who sat with her. Paul has a line for exactly this. Today: comforted to comfort.
screen: `SHE LEARNED IT AT HER OWN TABLE.`

segments.voice: It's how Paul opens his second letter to Corinth, the letter of the past few days. In the King James words: "Blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort; Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God." Count the comfort words in those two verses. Comfort, comforteth, comfort, comfort, comforted. Five times. Paul can't stop saying it. And follow where it goes. It starts with God, the God of all comfort. It reaches us in all our tribulation. And then it doesn't stop. That we may be able to comfort others. Comfort, in this letter, is not a pool you sit in. It's a river. It comes in so it can go out. And Paul isn't writing from a calm desk. A few verses later he tells the Corinthians that in Asia they were "pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life." So the comfort he means isn't advice from someone who's never been under it. It's the kind that's been tested. That's why the widow at the kitchen table helps. Not because she suffered, as if suffering were the qualification. Because she was comforted, and she remembers how it was done. Some readers see in this a picture of how a church works: the comforted becoming comforters, so that no one's comfort ends with them.

Here's the practice: comfort someone. Settle, and breathe. First, remember a time someone comforted you. Who was it? What did they actually do? Maybe they brought food, or sat in silence, or texted on the hard date without being asked. Hold that for a moment. Then think of someone going through something like what you went through. Ask what the comfort you received would look like, passed on to them. Pick one small, real thing, and when the bell ends, do it, or plan when you will. If you pray, you can name them before God. The bell holds the time.
Comforted to comfort. Paul's picture of God's comfort as a river: it reaches us in our trouble so it can reach others in theirs.
Your line: pass the comfort on. Today, do for one person the thing someone once did for you. Day one thousand four hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Christians comfort one another through visits, meals, prayer and simply sitting with people who grieve, and some churches run grief groups or care teams in which people who have been through a loss support others going through the same.

fork.setup: you're Paul. you've come through trouble so heavy you despaired even of life, and God comforted you. what do you write that the comfort was for?
options: proof that you were right all along.
so you can comfort others in any trouble.
a private gift, to keep to yourself.
fork.reveal: "that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God." the comfort is meant to move.
